# Dynamic Capabilities, Learning, and Renewal {#dynamic-capabilities}

In 1975 an engineer at Eastman Kodak, Steven Sasson, built one of the first
digital cameras. Kodak had world-class chemistry, an iconic brand, global
distribution, and deep research budgets: by any resource-based standard, a
formidable collection of valuable, rare, and hard-to-imitate assets. In January
2012 the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Its Japanese rival
Fujifilm faced the same collapse in demand for photographic film, yet emerged as
a diversified company with businesses in medical systems, pharmaceuticals,
cosmetics, and advanced materials. Netflix, meanwhile, cannibalized its own
DVD-by-mail business to build a streaming service, then reinvented itself again
as a producer of original content.

These cases expose a limitation of the theories in Chapter \@ref(resources).
Resource-based logic explains why a firm with superior resources outperforms its
rivals *at a point in time*. It says much less about how firms **renew** their
resources when technologies, customers, and competitors change, and why the very
resources that made a firm successful can become the reason it fails. This
chapter develops the theories that address renewal. We begin with the
**[dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) framework** and its main variants, then examine
**[absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity)** (how firms learn from outside), the tension between
**[exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation)** (how firms allocate attention between the new and
the known), and **[organizational ambidexterity](#ambidexterity)** (how firms try to do both). We
close each section with business cases drawn from the public record: Netflix,
Kodak and Fujifilm, Microsoft, and IBM (Table \@ref(tab:tab-dc-glance)).

```{r tab-dc-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "Dynamic capabilities", "How do firms integrate, build, and reconfigure competences as environments change?", "Firm", "Teece, Pisano, & Shuen (1997), Teece (2007)",
  "Dynamic capabilities as best practices", "Are dynamic capabilities idiosyncratic or common across firms?", "Firm / process", "Eisenhardt & Martin (2000)",
  "Capability hierarchy and learning", "Where do dynamic capabilities come from?", "Firm / routine", "Winter (2003), Zollo & Winter (2002)",
  "Core rigidities", "Why do strengths become weaknesses?", "Firm / project", "Leonard-Barton (1992)",
  "Absorptive capacity", "How do firms recognize, assimilate, and apply external knowledge?", "Firm / unit", "Cohen & Levinthal (1990), Zahra & George (2002)",

## Dynamic Capabilities Framework {#dynamic-capabilities-framework}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** In environments of rapid technological and market change,
sustained advantage depends less on the resources a firm owns than on its
**dynamic capabilities**: its ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure
internal and external competences to address changing environments.

**Origins.** Strategic management, building on evolutionary economics
[@nelson1982] and the [resource-based view](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)), @teece1997, elaborated in @teece2007
and @helfat2007, contrasting interpretation in @eisenhardt2000.

**Level of analysis.** Firm. Also specific organizational processes (product
development, acquisition integration, alliance management) and top management.

**Key constructs.** Ordinary (operational) capabilities, dynamic capabilities,
processes, positions, and paths, sensing, seizing, and transforming,
replication, imitation, path dependence, core rigidities.

**Boundary conditions.** Most consequential when environments change rapidly or
discontinuously. In stable environments, investment in dynamic capabilities may
cost more than it returns [@winter2003]. The form of effective dynamic
capabilities differs between moderately dynamic and high-velocity markets
[@eisenhardt2000].

**Related theories.** [Resource-based view](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Knowledge-based view](#knowledge-based-view) (Section \@ref(knowledge-based-view)),
[Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity),
[Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation),
[Ambidexterity](#ambidexterity),
[Diffusion of innovations](#diffusion-of-innovations) (Section \@ref(diffusion-of-innovations)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The framework's deepest root is the evolutionary theory of @nelson1982, which
replaced the neoclassical firm, a production function that maximizes profit,
with a firm that operates through **routines**: regular, predictable patterns of
activity that function as organizational memory and are the organizational
analogue of genes. Routines are efficient but sticky. Firms change mainly by
searching locally around what they already do, and markets select among firms
with different routines. From this perspective, a firm's capabilities are not
chosen at will. They are inherited from its history and modified incrementally.

@teece1997 combined this evolutionary view with resource-based logic. They
observed that the "winners" in global markets were firms that could demonstrate
"timely responsiveness and rapid and flexible product innovation, coupled with
the management capability to effectively coordinate and redeploy internal and
external competences" [@teece1997, p. 515]. Accumulating valuable assets is not
enough. Firms must also be able to change them. The term **dynamic** refers to
the capacity to renew competences so as to achieve congruence with a changing
business environment. **Capabilities** emphasises the role of strategic
management in adapting, integrating, and reconfiguring skills, resources, and
functional competences. Their formal definition has become the standard one:

::: {.definition}
**Dynamic capabilities** are "the firm's ability to integrate, build, and
reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing
environments" [@teece1997, p. 516].
:::

Teece and colleagues distinguished several layers of firm-specific assets, from
undifferentiated factors of production to the dynamic capabilities that change
them (Table \@ref(tab:tab-dc-terms)). The hierarchy foreshadows later work on
the distinction between ordinary and dynamic capabilities [@winter2003;
@teece2014].

```{r tab-dc-terms}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Term, ~`Meaning in Teece, Pisano, & Shuen (1997)`, ~`Business example`,
  "Factors of production", "Undifferentiated inputs available in disaggregated form in factor markets", "Commodity land, generic labour, standard machinery",
  "Resources", "Firm-specific assets that are difficult if not impossible to imitate", "Trade secrets, specialized production facilities, engineering experience",
  "Organizational routines / competences", "Firm-specific assets assembled in integrated clusters spanning individuals and groups so that they enable distinctive activities to be performed", "Quality management, miniaturization, systems integration",
  "Core competences", "The competences that define a firm's fundamental business", "Optics and imaging for a camera and copier maker",
  "Dynamic capabilities", "The ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences in rapidly changing environments", "Repeatedly moving into new product generations or business models",
  "Products", "Final goods and services produced by deploying the firm's competences", "Cameras, copiers, printers"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Layers of firm-specific assets in the dynamic capabilities framework (definitions paraphrased from Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997, p. 516).")
```

### Paradigms of competitive advantage

@teece1997 located their framework among four paradigms of strategy. Two
emphasise the exploitation of **market power**. The **competitive forces**
approach [@porter1980industry] holds that profitability is determined by
industry structure, and that firms should position themselves to defend against
the [five forces](#five-forces) (Section \@ref(five-forces)). The **strategic conflict** approach [@shapiro1989theory] uses game
theory to analyse how firms influence rivals' behaviour through investment,
pricing, signalling, and commitment. Two emphasise **efficiency**. The
**resource-based perspective** holds that firm-specific assets matter more than
industry position, because resources are heterogeneous and "sticky". The
**dynamic capabilities** approach adds that, when environments change, the
advantage lies in the capacity to renew those assets. Table
\@ref(tab:tab-dc-paradigms) summarises the comparison.

```{r tab-dc-paradigms}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Competitive forces`, ~`Strategic conflict`, ~`Resource-based view`, ~`Dynamic capabilities`,
  "Key source", "Porter (1980)", "Shapiro (1989)", "Wernerfelt (1984), Barney (1991)", "Teece, Pisano, & Shuen (1997)",
  "Source of rents", "Market power from favourable industry structure", "Market power from strategic moves against rivals", "Ricardian rents from scarce, firm-specific resources", "Schumpeterian rents from renewing resources and competences",
  "Unit of analysis", "Industry and firm position", "Firm and rivals (game)", "Resources and capabilities", "Processes, positions, and paths",
  "View of the firm", "Largely homogeneous within an industry", "Strategic actor with commitments", "Bundle of heterogeneous resources", "Evolving bundle of routines and competences",
  "Role of management", "Choose industry and position", "Out-manoeuvre rivals", "Acquire and protect valuable resources", "Sense, seize, and transform",
  "Time horizon", "Static (structure)", "Short-run interaction", "Comparative static", "Dynamic, path-dependent",
  "Typical prescription", "Enter attractive industries, build barriers", "Use commitment and signalling to deter rivals", "Exploit VRIO resources", "Invest in learning and reconfiguration"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Four paradigms of competitive advantage (organized following Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997).")
```

The paradigms are not mutually exclusive. Industry structure constrains what any
firm can earn. Game-theoretic interactions shape short-run outcomes. Resources
determine which firms can occupy attractive positions, and dynamic capabilities
determine whether those firms can move when the structure itself shifts. The
dynamic capabilities view is most distinctive when the main threat to profits is
not rivalry within a stable industry but **Schumpeterian** change: new
technologies and business models that make existing resources obsolete.

### Processes, positions, and paths

@teece1997 argued that a firm's distinctive competence and dynamic capabilities
are determined by three classes of factors (Table \@ref(tab:tab-dc-ppp)).

**Processes** are the way things are done in the firm: its routines and patterns
of current practice and learning. They serve three roles. **Coordination and
integration** is a static concept: how efficiently the firm coordinates activities
inside and outside its boundaries. **Learning** is a dynamic concept: how
repetition and experimentation allow tasks to be performed better and faster,
including through collaborations and partnerships. **Reconfiguration and
transformation** is the capacity to sense the need to change the asset structure
and to accomplish the internal and external transformation. Because change is
costly, firms need processes that reduce the cost of low-return change.

**Positions** are the firm's current endowments: technological assets,
complementary assets, financial assets, reputational assets, structural assets
(formal and informal organization and external linkages), institutional assets
(the regulatory and intellectual-property environment), market-structure assets,
and organizational boundaries (the degree of vertical, lateral, and horizontal
integration). Positions shape what the firm can do next. Complementary assets in
particular determine whether an innovator can profit from its innovation
[@teece1986].

**Paths** are the strategic alternatives available to the firm, which are shaped
by **path dependence**, a firm's previous investments and its repertoire of
routines constrain its future behaviour, and by **technological opportunities**,
which depend on the pace and direction of scientific discovery inside and outside
the industry. Path dependence also complicates learning: when many parameters
change at once, firms find it hard to identify causal relationships, so learning
tends to be local.

```{r tab-dc-ppp}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Factor, ~Elements, ~`Strategic question`, ~`Business illustration`,
  "Processes", "Coordination and integration, learning, reconfiguration and transformation", "How well do we coordinate, learn, and change?", "Repeatable product-launch and post-merger integration routines",
  "Positions", "Technological, complementary, financial, reputational, structural, institutional, and market assets. Organizational boundaries", "What do we hold now, and what does it enable?", "An installed customer base and global distribution that a new product can ride on",
  "Paths", "Path dependence, technological opportunities", "Which futures are open to us given our history?", "A film maker's chemistry know-how opening paths into cosmetics and pharmaceuticals"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Processes, positions, and paths (after Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997).")
```

### Replicability and imitability

If competences are valuable, why do firms struggle to copy them, including from
their own units? @teece1997 distinguish **replication**, transferring or
redeploying competences from one economic setting to another within the firm,
from **imitation**, replication by competitors. Replication is more than
information transfer because much of what a firm knows is tacit. The
organizational context in which a routine works is part of the routine. Imitation
is harder still, because imitators lack access to that context. The ease of
imitation is governed by the **appropriability regime**: the strength of
intellectual-property protection and the inherent replicability of the
technology. Process technologies hidden inside the factory are usually easier to
protect than product technologies that can be reverse-engineered once sold. These
arguments mirror the replication-imitation trade-off in the
[knowledge-based view](#knowledge-based-view) (Section \@ref(knowledge-based-view)) [@kogut1992].

### Microfoundations: sensing, seizing, and transforming

A decade later, @teece2007 disaggregated dynamic capabilities into three clusters
of activities, each with identifiable **microfoundations**, skills, processes,
procedures, organizational structures, decision rules, and disciplines:

- **Sensing** opportunities and threats: scanning, searching, and exploring
  technologies and markets. Directing internal R&D, tapping developments in
  science, suppliers, and complementors. Identifying changing customer needs and
  latent demand.
- **Seizing** opportunities: designing the business model and customer solution.
  Selecting enterprise boundaries and managing complements. Making timely,
  sometimes irreversible, investment decisions while avoiding decision biases,
  and building loyalty and commitment among employees.
- **Transforming** (managing threats and reconfiguring): continually realigning
  and recombining tangible and intangible assets, decentralizing and maintaining
  near-decomposable structures, managing cospecialized assets, governance and
  knowledge management.

@teece2014 sharpened the distinction between **ordinary capabilities**, which
allow a firm to perform current activities efficiently ("doing things right"), and
**dynamic capabilities**, which allow it to do the right things at the right time
by combining good strategy with the capacity to orchestrate resources. Ordinary
capabilities can often be bought or benchmarked. Dynamic capabilities rest on
signature processes and entrepreneurial management that are hard to imitate.
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dc-ssr) summarises the logic.

```{r fig-dc-ssr, fig.cap = "Microfoundations of dynamic capabilities. Sensing identifies opportunities and threats, seizing commits resources to address them, and transforming reconfigures the asset base. Managerial cognition and the firm's existing positions shape each step. Based on Teece (2007)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  E  [label = "Environmental change\\n(technology, demand,\\nregulation)", %s]
  S  [label = "Sensing\\n(scan, interpret,\\nlearn)", %s]
  Z  [label = "Seizing\\n(business model,\\ninvestment, boundaries)", %s]
  T  [label = "Transforming\\n(realign, recombine,\\nreconfigure assets)", %s]
  F  [label = "Evolutionary fitness\\nand sustained\\nperformance", %s]
  M  [label = "Managerial cognition\\nand leadership", %s]
  P  [label = "Existing positions\\nand paths", %s]
  E -> S -> Z -> T -> F
  M -> S [style = dashed]
  M -> Z [style = dashed]
  P -> Z [style = dashed]
  P -> T [style = dashed]
  T -> S [label = " renewed\\n asset base", style = dashed, constraint = false]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome,
   node_moderator, node_moderator))
```

### Dynamic capabilities as best practices

@eisenhardt2000 offered an influential reinterpretation. They argued that dynamic
capabilities are not vague, idiosyncratic abilities but **specific, identifiable
processes**: product development, strategic decision making, alliancing,
acquisition integration, resource allocation, and knowledge brokering. Because
effective versions of these processes share common features across firms, dynamic
capabilities exhibit **equifinality** (firms can reach them from different
starting points) and substantial **commonality**: they resemble "best practices".
It follows that dynamic capabilities are *necessary but not sufficient* for
competitive advantage: advantage comes from the **resource configurations** that
firms create with them, sooner, more astutely, or more fortuitously than rivals.

The form of effective dynamic capabilities, they argued, depends on **market
dynamism**. In **moderately dynamic** markets, where change is frequent but
predictable, dynamic capabilities resemble traditional routines: detailed,
analytic, stable processes with predictable outcomes that rely on existing
knowledge. In **high-velocity** markets, where change is nonlinear and
unpredictable, effective dynamic capabilities are **simple rules** and
experiential processes that rely on rapidly created new knowledge, prototyping,
and iterative execution. Their outcomes are unpredictable, and they are
inherently fragile. Learning mechanisms such as repeated practice, codification,
learning from small failures, and pacing guide their evolution (Table \@ref(tab:tab-dc-views)).

```{r tab-dc-views}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Teece, Pisano, & Shuen (1997), Teece (2007)`, ~`Eisenhardt & Martin (2000)`,
  "Nature of dynamic capabilities", "Firm-specific, partly tacit, embedded in processes and managerial skill", "Specific, identifiable processes with common features across firms",
  "Heterogeneity", "Idiosyncratic, hard to imitate", "Commonalities across firms (best practices), equifinality",
  "Link to advantage", "Can be a direct source of sustained advantage", "Necessary but not sufficient, advantage lies in resulting resource configurations",
  "Role of market dynamism", "Most valuable in rapidly changing environments", "Form differs: detailed routines (moderate) vs. simple rules (high velocity)",
  "Role of managers", "Entrepreneurial sensing, seizing, and transforming", "Designing and executing effective processes",
  "Sustainability", "Durable if microfoundations are hard to replicate", "Advantage often temporary in high-velocity markets"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Two conversations about dynamic capabilities (see Peteraf, Di Stefano, & Verona, 2013).")
```

::: {.debate}
**Two conversations or one?** @peteraf2013 showed through a co-citation analysis
that the dynamic capabilities literature had split into two largely separate
conversations, anchored by @teece1997 and @eisenhardt2000, which disagree about
whether dynamic capabilities can underpin *sustained* advantage and under what
market conditions. They proposed a contingent reconciliation: the two views can
be integrated once boundary conditions such as market dynamism and the level of
the capability are made explicit. Critics have also raised a **tautology**
concern similar to the one levelled at the RBV: if a dynamic capability is defined
by successful change, its link to performance is true by definition. A related
**infinite-regress** problem asks whether there are capabilities to change
dynamic capabilities, and capabilities to change *those*. @collis1994 noted that
any higher-order capability can be trumped by one at a still higher order.
@schilke2018, reviewing the empirical literature, found growing evidence that
dynamic capabilities are associated with performance, often indirectly through
changes in operational capabilities, while urging clearer measurement and
stronger causal designs.
:::

### The capability hierarchy and learning mechanisms

@winter2003 clarified the concept by distinguishing **zero-order** (ordinary)
capabilities, those that permit a firm to make a living in the short term by
producing and selling the same product to the same customers at the same scale,
from **first-order** dynamic capabilities that change the product, the production
process, the scale, or the customers served, and from **higher-order**
capabilities that change the dynamic capabilities themselves. He made two further
points that are easy to miss. First, not all change requires a dynamic capability:
firms can change through **ad hoc problem solving**, which is non-routine and
creative but not patterned. Second, dynamic capabilities are **costly**, they
require long-term commitments to specialized resources and people, so whether
they pay off depends on how often and how predictably the environment changes.
A firm in a stable market may rationally rely on ad hoc change.

Where do dynamic capabilities come from? @zollo2002 defined a dynamic capability
as a learned and stable pattern of collective activity through which an
organization systematically generates and modifies its operating routines in
pursuit of improved effectiveness. They traced its origins to three **learning
mechanisms** of increasing deliberateness and cost:

1. **Experience accumulation**: tacit learning by doing, as routines are
   repeated.
2. **Knowledge articulation**: making knowledge explicit through collective
   discussion, debriefings, and performance reviews.
3. **Knowledge codification**: writing knowledge down in manuals, decision
   tools, checklists, and software.

The more deliberate mechanisms are especially valuable when the relevant tasks
are **infrequent**, **heterogeneous**, and **causally ambiguous**: conditions under
which experience alone teaches poorly. Post-acquisition integration is their
example: few firms do enough acquisitions for experience alone to be a reliable
teacher, and each deal differs from the last. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dc-hierarchy)
combines Winter's hierarchy with Zollo and Winter's learning mechanisms.

```{r fig-dc-hierarchy, fig.cap = "The capability hierarchy. Learning mechanisms generate and modify dynamic capabilities, which in turn modify the operating routines (ordinary capabilities) that produce current performance. Based on Winter (2003) and Zollo and Winter (2002).", fig.height = 5}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  L1 [label = "Experience\\naccumulation", %s]
  L2 [label = "Knowledge\\narticulation", %s]
  L3 [label = "Knowledge\\ncodification", %s]
  D  [label = "Dynamic capabilities\\n(first-order: change product,\\nprocess, scale, customers)", %s]
  O  [label = "Operating routines\\n(zero-order / ordinary\\ncapabilities)", %s]
  P  [label = "Current performance\\nand adaptation", %s]
  X  [label = "Frequency, heterogeneity,\\nand causal ambiguity\\nof the task", %s]
  L1 -> D
  L2 -> D
  L3 -> D
  D -> O [label = " generate\\n and modify"]
  O -> P
  X -> L2 [style = dashed]
  X -> L3 [style = dashed]
  P -> L1 [label = " experience", style = dashed, constraint = false]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_outcome, node_moderator), rankdir = "TB")
```

@helfat2003 added a life-cycle perspective. Capabilities are founded, developed,
and reach maturity. When environments change, they may branch into
**retirement**, **retrenchment**, **renewal**, **replication** (in another market),
**redeployment** (to a related market), or **recombination** (with other
capabilities). The capability life cycle explains why a firm's capability
portfolio has a history and why the same capability can be an asset in one era and
a burden in the next.

### Core rigidities

@leonardbarton1992 identified the paradox at the heart of capability renewal. In
a field study of new product development projects, she found that the **core
capabilities** that distinguish a firm, rooted in employee knowledge and skills,
technical systems, managerial systems, and values and norms, simultaneously
enhance projects that fit them and hinder projects that do not. The same
capabilities become **core rigidities** when the firm needs to move in a new
direction: skills that were celebrated become narrow, systems that were efficient
become constraints, and values that motivated people become filters that screen
out unfamiliar ideas.

Research on technological change reinforces the point. Discontinuities that are
**competence-destroying**, rendering existing skills obsolete, tend to be
introduced by new entrants and to hurt incumbents, whereas **competence-enhancing**
discontinuities tend to favour incumbents [@tushman1986]. Even seemingly modest
**architectural innovations**, which change how known components are linked,
can defeat incumbents whose communication channels and information filters are
organized around the old architecture [@henderson1990]. And capability is not
the only constraint: in their study of Polaroid's move into digital imaging,
@tripsas2000 showed that the firm developed substantial technical capability but
that managerial beliefs about the business model, rooted in its instant-film
heritage, shaped how it deployed that capability. **Cognition** as well as
capability determines whether a firm can change.

::: {.business-case}
**Kodak and Fujifilm.** Both firms faced the same competence-destroying
discontinuity as digital imaging displaced chemical film. Kodak was not ignorant
of the technology, its own engineer had built an early digital camera in 1975,
and it introduced digital cameras and services. But its economics, organization,
and identity were built around film, processing, and paper, and digital products
offered nothing comparable to that business. The company filed for Chapter 11
protection in 2012 and emerged as a much smaller firm. Fujifilm, under
long-serving chief executive Shigetaka Komori, restructured its film operations
and asked which of its underlying competences, chemistry, thin films, coatings,
precision manufacturing, and image processing, could be redeployed. It moved
into medical imaging and pharmaceuticals (including the acquisition of Toyama
Chemical in 2008), launched a cosmetics line built on its expertise in collagen
and antioxidants, and supplied optical films for flat-panel displays. In Helfat
and Peteraf's terms, Fujifilm **redeployed** and **recombined** capabilities.
In Teece's terms, it sensed the threat and transformed its asset base, rather
than defending a core that had become a rigidity.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Netflix: renewing the business model twice.** Netflix was founded in 1997 as a
DVD-by-mail rental service and built ordinary capabilities in logistics,
subscription billing, and recommendation algorithms. In 2007 it launched
streaming, a technology that would eventually cannibalize its own core. In 2011
it announced a plan to split the DVD business into a separate service called
Qwikster, provoking a customer backlash. The plan was reversed within weeks: a
reminder that seizing is risky and that reconfiguration has costs. Netflix then
moved into original programming, beginning with *House of Cards* in 2013, which
required capabilities in content development, talent relations, and global
production that a distributor had not needed. It expanded into most countries in
2016 and closed its DVD business in 2023. Read through Teece's framework, Netflix
sensed shifts in broadband and consumer behaviour, seized them by committing to
streaming and original content before they were profitable, and transformed its
asset base from warehouses and discs to software, data, and intellectual
property. Its rival Blockbuster, which filed for bankruptcy in 2010, illustrates
the alternative path.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Microsoft's turn to the cloud.** When Satya Nadella became chief executive in
2014, Microsoft's profits were anchored in Windows and Office licences, and it had
struggled in mobile devices and search. Under the banner "mobile-first,
cloud-first", the company shifted investment toward its Azure cloud platform and
subscription software (Office 365), wrote down its phone business, made its
software available on rival platforms, and embraced open-source technologies it
had once opposed, later acquiring LinkedIn (2016) and GitHub (2018). Nadella
emphasised that the strategic shift depended on a cultural one, built around a
"growth mindset" [@nadella2017]. In dynamic capabilities terms, Microsoft did not
abandon its positions, enterprise relationships, developer ecosystems, and
software engineering, but **recombined** them with new cloud infrastructure. The
transformation of managerial systems and values, Leonard-Barton's deepest layers
of capability, was as important as the technology.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Firms with more deliberate learning mechanisms (articulation and
  codification) for acquisition integration will achieve better post-acquisition
  performance, especially when acquisitions are infrequent and heterogeneous
  [@zollo2002].
- *H2.* The effect of dynamic capabilities on firm performance will be mediated by
  changes in operational capabilities [@schilke2018].
- *H3.* Detailed, codified product development routines will improve performance
  in moderately dynamic markets but not in high-velocity markets, where simple
  rules will be more effective [@eisenhardt2000].

**Designs.** Longitudinal case studies of renewal, panel studies of firms facing
exogenous shocks (deregulation, technological discontinuities), event studies of
reconfiguration announcements, simulation models of routine evolution, survey
scales of sensing, seizing, and transforming validated against behavioural
indicators.

**Measures.** Frequency and speed of product-line renewal. Acquisition and
alliance experience and the presence of integration manuals or teams. R&D
reallocation across technology classes. Top-management attention to emerging
issues (text analysis of letters to shareholders or earnings calls).

**Data sources.** Patent and product-launch databases, SDC for acquisitions and
alliances, annual reports and earnings-call transcripts, industry case archives.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Defining capability by outcome.** It is tempting to infer that a firm that
adapted successfully "had" dynamic capabilities and one that failed did not. This
is circular. Measure the capability *before* the change, the presence of
sensing processes, investment rules, learning mechanisms, and test whether it
predicts adaptation, ideally among firms facing the same shock. Remember also
Winter's point that change can happen without a dynamic capability, through ad
hoc problem solving or luck.
:::

## Absorptive Capacity {#absorptive-capacity}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** A firm's ability to recognize the value of new external
knowledge, assimilate it, and apply it to commercial ends, its **absorptive
capacity**, is largely a function of its prior related knowledge, and therefore
develops cumulatively and path-dependently.

**Origins.** Economics of innovation and organization theory, @cohen1990,
reconceptualized by @zahra2002.

**Level of analysis.** Firm and business unit. Also individuals and teams who
act as gatekeepers and boundary spanners.

**Key constructs.** Prior related knowledge, acquisition, assimilation,
transformation, exploitation, potential vs. realized absorptive capacity,
activation triggers, social integration mechanisms, regimes of appropriability.

**Boundary conditions.** Most important where valuable knowledge is generated
outside the firm (by universities, suppliers, customers, or rivals) and is
partly tacit or complex.

**Related theories.** [Knowledge-based view](#knowledge-based-view) (Section \@ref(knowledge-based-view)),
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework),
[Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation),
[Diffusion of innovations](#diffusion-of-innovations) (Section \@ref(diffusion-of-innovations)).
:::

### Core logic

@cohen1990 began from an observation about learning in individuals: the ability to
learn new things depends on what one already knows, because new knowledge is
understood by relating it to existing knowledge structures. Organizations are no
different. A firm's **absorptive capacity** is its ability to recognize the value
of new, external information, assimilate it, and apply it to commercial ends.
Because it depends on prior related knowledge, absorptive capacity is
**cumulative**, investing in it today makes tomorrow's learning easier, and
**path-dependent**. A firm that stops investing in a field may find itself
**locked out**: it can no longer recognize the significance of developments it
once could have exploited.

Two implications have been especially influential. First, a firm's own R&D does
more than produce inventions. It also builds the capacity to understand and use
other organizations' inventions. Internal research and external sourcing are
therefore complements rather than substitutes. Second, organizational absorptive
capacity is not simply the sum of individuals' knowledge. It depends on
**gatekeepers** and **boundary spanners** who translate external knowledge for
internal use, and on internal communication structures that move knowledge to
where it can be applied. Some overlap of knowledge across units helps
communication, while diversity of backgrounds increases the range of external
developments the firm can recognize.

### Potential and realized absorptive capacity

@zahra2002 reconceptualized absorptive capacity as a dynamic capability with four
dimensions grouped into two components. **Potential absorptive capacity
(PACAP)** comprises **acquisition** (identifying and acquiring external knowledge)
and **assimilation** (analysing, interpreting, and understanding it). **Realized
absorptive capacity (RACAP)** comprises **transformation** (combining new and
existing knowledge) and **exploitation** (applying the result to create new or
improved products, processes, and competences). The distinction explains why
firms that are good at scanning the environment do not necessarily profit from
what they find: PACAP without RACAP generates costs without returns, while RACAP
without PACAP can produce short-term gains but leaves the firm exposed to
competence traps. The ratio of realized to potential capacity is an **efficiency
factor** that varies across firms.

The model also specifies contingencies (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dc-acap)).
**Activation triggers**, crises, technological shifts, regulatory changes,
intensify the search for external knowledge. **Social integration mechanisms**,
formal and informal, reduce the gap between potential and realized capacity by
spreading knowledge within the firm. **Regimes of appropriability**, the
strength of intellectual-property protection and the inimitability of the
resulting knowledge, determine whether realized capacity translates into
sustained advantage.

```{r fig-dc-acap, fig.cap = "Potential and realized absorptive capacity. External knowledge sources and prior experience feed potential capacity (acquisition and assimilation). Social integration mechanisms convert it into realized capacity (transformation and exploitation), which yields advantage when appropriability regimes protect the results. Adapted from Zahra and George (2002)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  K  [label = "External knowledge\\nsources and\\nprior experience", %s]
  P  [label = "Potential ACAP\\n(acquisition,\\nassimilation)", %s]
  R  [label = "Realized ACAP\\n(transformation,\\nexploitation)", %s]
  C  [label = "Competitive advantage\\n(flexibility, innovation,\\nperformance)", %s]
  AT [label = "Activation\\ntriggers", %s]
  SI [label = "Social integration\\nmechanisms", %s]
  AR [label = "Regimes of\\nappropriability", %s]
  K -> P -> R -> C
  AT -> P [style = dashed]
  SI -> R [style = dashed]
  AR -> C [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome,
   node_moderator, node_moderator, node_moderator))
```

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: [open innovation](#open-innovation) (Section \@ref(open-innovation)) in a consumer-goods firm.** A packaged-food
company launches an open-innovation portal and a corporate venture unit to scout
start-ups and university labs (potential absorptive capacity). Two years later,
the scouting team has catalogued hundreds of technologies, yet few have reached
products. Diagnosis using Zahra and George's model points to weak realized
capacity: the scouts report to a corporate strategy office with no product
responsibility, business-unit R&D teams lack the food-science expertise to
evaluate fermentation-based proteins, and there is no forum in which scouts and
product managers jointly prioritize opportunities. Remedies follow the model:
rotate R&D staff through the scouting unit, create joint stage-gate reviews (a
social integration mechanism), and invest selectively in internal research in
the most promising fields to build the prior knowledge needed to evaluate them.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Measuring absorptive capacity with R&D intensity alone.** R&D spending is the
most common proxy, but it captures, at best, investment in potential capacity in
technical domains. It misses non-technical knowledge (market, regulatory), the
transformation and exploitation components, and the internal integration
mechanisms that Cohen and Levinthal themselves emphasised. Combine input measures
with process indicators (boundary-spanning roles, cross-unit forums) and outcome
measures (citations to external knowledge in the firm's patents, speed of
adopting external innovations).
:::

## Exploration and Exploitation {#exploration-exploitation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Adaptive systems must divide resources between **exploration** of
new possibilities and **exploitation** of old certainties. Because the returns to
exploitation are surer, faster, and closer, learning processes tend to favour it,
which improves short-run performance but can be self-destructive in the long run.

**Origins.** Organizational learning and behavioural theory of the firm,
@march1991, @levinthal1993, @levitt1988.

**Level of analysis.** Individual, organization, and population of
organizations.

**Key constructs.** Exploration, exploitation, competency trap, success trap,
failure trap, temporal, spatial, and failure myopia, mutual learning.

**Boundary conditions.** The tension is sharpest when resources are scarce,
when exploration and exploitation require different structures and cultures,
and when environments change.

**Related theories.** [Ambidexterity](#ambidexterity),
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework),
[Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity),
[Bounded rationality](#bounded-rationality) (Section \@ref(bounded-rationality)).
:::

### Core logic

@march1991 framed organizational adaptation as a choice between two kinds of
activity. **Exploration** includes search, variation, risk taking,
experimentation, play, flexibility, discovery, and innovation. **Exploitation**
includes refinement, choice, production, efficiency, selection, implementation,
and execution. Both are essential, but they compete for scarce resources and
they have different return profiles: the returns to exploitation are positive,
proximate, and predictable, whereas the returns to exploration are uncertain,
distant, and often negative. Because organizations learn from feedback, and
feedback from exploitation arrives sooner and more reliably, adaptive processes
tend to refine exploitation faster than exploration. The result is effective in
the short run and potentially self-destructive in the long run.

March illustrated the argument with a model of **mutual learning** between an
organizational code (beliefs embodied in procedures and norms) and its members.
The code learns from individuals whose beliefs are closer to reality, and
individuals are socialized to the code. Fast socialization speeds convergence but
eliminates the diversity from which the code learns. Slower learners, and a
moderate turnover of personnel, preserve useful variety and improve long-run
knowledge. Diversity, in other words, is an exploration resource.

@levitt1988 had already identified the **competency trap**: favourable
performance with an inferior procedure leads an organization to accumulate more
experience with it, which keeps experience with a superior procedure too low to
make it rewarding to use. @levinthal1993 generalized the problem as the **myopia
of learning**. Learning tends to overlook the long run (**temporal myopia**),
distant parts of the organization or environment (**spatial myopia**), and failures
(**failure myopia**). Two dynamic traps follow. In a **success trap**, exploitation
yields success, which encourages more exploitation, which drives out exploration.
In a **failure trap**, exploration produces failure, which prompts further search
for something new, which produces further failure, so the organization never
stays long enough to become competent at anything.

### Mechanism: an illustrative simulation

The exploration-exploitation problem has a precise analogue in the
**multi-armed bandit** problem of decision theory and reinforcement learning
[@sutton2018]. A decision maker repeatedly chooses among options with unknown,
possibly changing payoffs. Choosing the option with the highest estimated payoff
exploits current knowledge. Choosing another option explores. A simple policy,
**$\varepsilon$-greedy**, exploits with probability $1 - \varepsilon$ and explores
at random with probability $\varepsilon$.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dc-bandit) applies the policy to a stylised firm. The firm
knows its core business well. An emerging opportunity starts with low payoffs
but improves over time, while the core business slowly declines. Unfamiliar
options are initially valued pessimistically, as they often are inside
established firms. A pure exploiter ($\varepsilon = 0$) earns the most early on and then falls
into a competency trap: it never learns enough about the emerging option to
switch. A heavy explorer ($\varepsilon = 0.3$) pays a large exploration tax while the
environment is stable, but detects and moves to the emerging opportunity fastest
once it improves. A moderate explorer ($\varepsilon = 0.1$) gives up a little early
payoff and adapts more slowly, but it does adapt.

```{r fig-dc-bandit, fig.cap = "Illustrative bandit simulation of exploration and exploitation. A firm chooses each period among a known core business that slowly declines, an emerging opportunity that improves, and four other options. The pure exploiter wins early but falls into a competency trap. Exploration pays off once the environment shifts.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1991)
sim_bandit <- function(eps, runs = 400, n_periods = 400, K = 6, alpha = 0.1) {
  set.seed(1991)                                      # common random environments across policies
  t_seq <- seq_len(n_periods)
  core  <- ifelse(t_seq <= 150, 1, pmax(0.3, 1 - 0.7 * (t_seq - 150) / 200))   # declining core
  emerg <- ifelse(t_seq <= 100, 0.2, pmin(2, 0.2 + 1.8 * (t_seq - 100) / 200)) # rising opportunity
  other <- matrix(rnorm(runs * (K - 2), 0, 0.5), runs, K - 2)                   # other options
  Q <- cbind(1, matrix(-0.5, runs, K - 1))            # core known; unfamiliar options undervalued
  reward <- matrix(NA_real_, runs, n_periods)
  for (t in t_seq) {
    mu <- cbind(core[t], emerg[t], other)
    greedy <- max.col(Q, ties.method = "random")
    choice <- ifelse(runif(runs) < eps, sample.int(K, runs, replace = TRUE), greedy)
    idx <- cbind(seq_len(runs), choice)
    r <- rnorm(runs, mu[idx], 1)
    Q[idx] <- Q[idx] + alpha * (r - Q[idx])           # recency-weighted learning
    reward[, t] <- r
  }
  data.frame(period = t_seq, reward = colMeans(reward), eps = eps)
}
bandit <- bind_rows(lapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.3), sim_bandit)) |>
  group_by(eps) |>
  mutate(smooth = as.numeric(stats::filter(reward, rep(1 / 15, 15), sides = 1))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(policy = factor(eps, levels = c(0, 0.1, 0.3),
                         labels = c("Pure exploitation (rate 0)", "Moderate exploration (rate 0.1)",
                                    "Heavy exploration (rate 0.3)")))
ggplot(filter(bandit, !is.na(smooth)), aes(period, smooth, colour = policy)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 100, xmax = 300, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ink[["grid"]], alpha = 0.45) +
  annotate("text", x = 200, y = 1.95, label = "Environment shifts:\ncore declines, new option improves",
           size = 3.1, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.95) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 2.1)) +
  labs(x = "Period", y = "Average payoff (15-period moving avg.)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Exploitation wins early, exploration wins when the world changes",
       caption = "Stylised simulation: 400 simulated firms per policy, 6 options, learning rate 0.1, payoff noise sd = 1.") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dc-tradeoff) varies the exploration rate systematically and
reports average payoffs in the stable early phase, after the environmental shift,
and over the whole horizon. Early payoffs fall monotonically with exploration:
exploration is a tax on current performance. Late payoffs rise sharply as soon as
the firm explores at all and fall again when exploration becomes excessive. The
whole-horizon payoff is an inverted U: too little exploration produces a
competency trap. Too much produces the failure-trap pattern of never
capitalizing on what has been learned. The optimal balance depends on how
quickly and how much the environment changes: the core contingency in March's
argument.

```{r fig-dc-tradeoff, fig.cap = "Illustrative trade-off between exploration and performance in the same stylised bandit environment. Exploration lowers early payoffs but raises payoffs after the environment shifts. Total payoff peaks at an intermediate exploration rate.", fig.height = 3.9}
eps_grid <- c(0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5)
tradeoff <- bind_rows(lapply(eps_grid, sim_bandit)) |>
  group_by(eps) |>
  summarise(`Early, stable phase (periods 1-100)` = mean(reward[period <= 100]),
            `After the shift (periods 301-400)` = mean(reward[period > 300]),
            `Whole horizon (periods 1-400)` = mean(reward)) |>
  pivot_longer(-eps, names_to = "window", values_to = "payoff") |>
  mutate(window = factor(window, levels = c("Early, stable phase (periods 1-100)",
                                            "After the shift (periods 301-400)",
                                            "Whole horizon (periods 1-400)")))
ggplot(tradeoff, aes(eps, payoff, colour = window)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "Exploration rate (share of choices made at random)", y = "Average payoff per period",
       colour = NULL, title = "The exploration tax and the exploration dividend",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (same environment as the previous figure). 400 Simulated firms per exploration rate.") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

The simulation is deliberately simple, but it reproduces three of the theory's
core claims: exploitation is rewarded sooner and more reliably. A firm that learns
only from its own experience with familiar options can be trapped by its own
competence, and the right balance is contingent on environmental change. It also
illustrates why the balance is hard to manage in practice: the cost of exploration
is visible in every quarterly report, whereas the cost of under-exploration is
visible only after the environment shifts.

### Evidence and extensions

Empirical and conceptual work has refined March's framing in several ways.
@benner2003 showed that **process management** practices, such as quality
programmes and process certification, increase exploitation and, if applied
throughout the organization, crowd out exploration. They argued for insulating
exploratory units from such practices. @gupta2006 asked whether exploration and
exploitation are two ends of one continuum (competing for the same resources) or
**orthogonal** activities that can both be high, and concluded that the answer
depends on the level of analysis and on whether the activities draw on the same
scarce resources. @lavie2010 reviewed the literature and distinguished several
ways firms balance the two: **organizational separation** (different units),
**temporal separation** (alternating over time), and **domain separation**
(exploring in some domains, such as alliances, while exploiting in others).

### Disruptive innovation {#dc-disruptive-innovation}

@christensen1997 provided a vivid, partly complementary account of why successful
firms under-explore. In studies of the disk-drive industry and other sectors, he
distinguished **sustaining** technologies, which improve products along dimensions
mainstream customers already value, from **disruptive** technologies, which
initially underperform on those dimensions but offer other benefits (simplicity,
convenience, lower cost) valued by fringe or new customers. Incumbents typically
lead in sustaining innovation. They lose to disruptive innovations not because
they are badly managed but because good management, listening to the best
customers, investing in the highest-margin opportunities, directs resources away
from small, low-margin markets that later grow. In the language of this chapter,
the firm's resource-allocation processes are an exploitation machine. Christensen's
remedy, an autonomous organization with a cost structure suited to the new market,
is a form of structural ambidexterity.

::: {.debate}
**How general is disruption?** The theory of [disruptive innovation](#disruptive-innovation) (Section \@ref(disruptive-innovation)) has been widely
applied, some argue over-applied, to any successful entrant. Scholars have
questioned whether disruption can be identified *ex ante* rather than only in
hindsight, and have noted incumbents that responded successfully to apparently
disruptive threats. For research purposes, the theory is most useful when its
specific conditions are stated and measured: an entrant whose initial product
underperforms on mainstream attributes, a performance trajectory that eventually
meets mainstream needs, and incumbent resource-allocation processes that
systematically favour existing customers.
:::

## Organizational Ambidexterity {#ambidexterity}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Organizations can achieve long-run success by simultaneously
exploiting existing competences and exploring new ones: through structurally
separate units integrated by senior leadership, through a context that enables
individuals to divide their own time, or through sequential shifts over time.

**Origins.** Organization theory and strategy, @tushman1996, @oreilly2004,
@gibson2004, reviewed in @raisch2008 and @oreilly2013.

**Level of analysis.** Firm, business unit, senior team, and individual.

**Key constructs.** Structural ambidexterity, contextual ambidexterity
(alignment and adaptability), sequential (temporal) ambidexterity, senior team
integration, organizational context (discipline, stretch, support, trust).

**Boundary conditions.** Benefits are greatest for firms with the resources to
sustain both activities and in environments that are dynamic. Small firms and
stable environments may benefit more from focus.

**Related theories.** [Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation),
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework),
[Contingency theory](#contingency-theory) (Section \@ref(contingency-theory)),
[Upper echelons theory](#upper-echelons-theory) (Section \@ref(upper-echelons-theory)).
:::

### Three forms of ambidexterity

@tushman1996 argued that long-term success requires firms to compete in mature
markets, where cost, efficiency, and incremental innovation matter, while also
developing new products and services for emerging markets, where experimentation,
speed, and flexibility matter. Because these require different structures,
processes, and cultures, they proposed the **ambidextrous organization**: separate
units for exploration and exploitation, each with its own alignment of people,
structure, and culture, held together by a senior team and a common strategic
intent. @oreilly2004 reported that firms using such structures were more
successful at launching breakthrough innovations without sacrificing the
existing business than firms that relied on functional designs, cross-functional
teams embedded in the existing organization, or unsupported independent units.
The key was integration at the top: separate units, but a senior team that
shared resources and resolved conflicts between them.

@gibson2004 proposed a different route. **Contextual ambidexterity** is the
behavioural capacity to demonstrate both **alignment** (coherence among
activities in pursuit of current goals) and **adaptability** (the capacity to
reconfigure activities quickly to meet changing demands) across an entire
business unit. It arises not from structural separation but from an
organizational context that combines **performance management** (discipline and
stretch) with **social support** (support and trust), allowing individuals to
decide for themselves how to divide time between conflicting demands. In their
study of business units in multinational firms, contextual ambidexterity
mediated the relationship between organizational context and performance.

A third form, **sequential ambidexterity**, has firms shift their structures over
time, exploring in one period, exploiting in the next, which may suit slower
environments or smaller firms [@oreilly2013]. Table \@ref(tab:tab-dc-ambi)
compares the three.

```{r tab-dc-ambi}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Structural ambidexterity`, ~`Contextual ambidexterity`, ~`Sequential ambidexterity`,
  "Key sources", "Tushman & O'Reilly (1996), O'Reilly & Tushman (2004)", "Gibson & Birkinshaw (2004)", "O'Reilly & Tushman (2013)",
  "How the tension is resolved", "Separate units for exploration and exploitation", "Individuals divide time between alignment and adaptability", "The organization alternates between modes over time",
  "Where integration happens", "Senior team, shared vision, targeted linkages", "Organizational context and individual judgement", "Leadership-driven transitions",
  "Key enablers", "Distinct structures, metrics, and cultures, senior-team integration", "Discipline, stretch, support, trust", "Capacity to restructure, change management",
  "Best suited to", "Large firms facing discontinuous change", "Business units with incremental, adjacent innovation", "Slower-moving environments, smaller firms",
  "Main risk", "Isolation or starvation of exploratory units", "Overload, exploitation crowds out exploration", "Disruption and lost momentum at each shift"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Three forms of organizational ambidexterity.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The evidence broadly supports a positive association between ambidexterity and
performance, with important qualifications. @he2004, in a study of manufacturing
firms, found that the *interaction* of exploration and exploitation was positively
related to sales growth, while a *relative imbalance* between them was negatively
related: an early direct test of the ambidexterity hypothesis. Reviews by
@raisch2008 and @oreilly2013 conclude that the benefits of ambidexterity depend on
environmental dynamism, competitive intensity, and firm size and resources, and
that ambidexterity is better understood as a **dynamic capability** of senior
leadership than as a structural formula. They also note persistent measurement
debates: whether to combine exploration and exploitation additively (combined
dimension) or as a difference (balance dimension), and at which level to measure
them.

::: {.business-case}
**IBM's Emerging Business Opportunities process.** IBM's history illustrates both
the danger of core rigidities and the use of ambidextrous structures. In the early
1990s the company suffered heavy losses as the computer industry shifted away from
mainframes. Louis Gerstner, who became chief executive in 1993, reversed plans to
break the company into independent units and instead repositioned it around
integrated solutions and services [@gerstner2002]. Later, IBM created an
**Emerging Business Opportunities (EBO)** process, begun in 2000, to protect
promising new businesses from the short-term metrics of the established
divisions: EBOs received dedicated leaders, separate funding, milestones suited to
exploration, and regular senior-executive review [@harreld2007]. Subsequent
portfolio moves, selling the personal computer business to Lenovo in 2005,
acquiring Red Hat in 2019, and spinning off its managed-infrastructure services
business as Kyndryl in 2021, show sequential reconfiguration of the asset base.
@harreld2007 interpret IBM's approach as an attempt to build dynamic capabilities
in the senior leadership system rather than relying on any single
reorganization.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The positive effect of exploratory innovation on firm performance will be
  stronger in more dynamic environments, and the positive effect of exploitative
  innovation stronger in more competitive environments.
- *H2.* Structural separation of exploratory units will improve their innovation
  outcomes only when the senior team shares integrative goals and a common reward
  system.
- *H3.* Business units whose context combines high discipline and stretch with high
  support and trust will exhibit higher contextual ambidexterity, which will
  mediate the effect of context on unit performance [@gibson2004].

**Designs.** Panel studies coding exploration and exploitation from patents
(new versus familiar technology classes), product launches, or alliance types,
multilevel surveys of business units, field experiments on time allocation,
agent-based simulations in the tradition of @march1991.

**Measures.** Exploration and exploitation scales (e.g., following @he2004).
Patent-based measures of search distance. Share of R&D budget devoted to new
domains. Balance and combined ambidexterity indices.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating ambidexterity as "more of everything".** Ambidexterity does not mean
maximizing both exploration and exploitation everywhere. The theory's core insight
is that the two compete for scarce resources and require different structures and
cultures, so they must be deliberately separated, sequenced, or contextually
balanced, and integrated by leaders who manage the tension. Studies that simply
add exploration and exploitation scores without modelling that tension, or that
ignore resource constraints and environmental conditions, test a weaker claim
than the theory makes.
:::

## Chapter Summary {#dynamic-capabilities-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- **Dynamic capabilities** are the firm's ability to integrate, build, and
  reconfigure competences to address changing environments. They rest on
  **processes**, are shaped by **positions**, and are constrained by **paths**
  [@teece1997].
- @teece2007 decomposes them into **sensing**, **seizing**, and **transforming**,
  each with microfoundations in managerial skill, processes, and structure.
- @eisenhardt2000 view dynamic capabilities as identifiable **best practices** whose
  form depends on market dynamism. Advantage comes from the resource configurations
  they create.
- A **capability hierarchy** separates ordinary from dynamic capabilities
  [@winter2003]. Dynamic capabilities are built through **deliberate learning**
  [@zollo2002] and evolve over a **life cycle** [@helfat2003].
- Core capabilities can become **core rigidities** [@leonardbarton1992]. Cognition as
  well as capability shapes adaptation [@tripsas2000].
- **Absorptive capacity** depends on prior related knowledge. **Potential** capacity
  must be converted into **realized** capacity through integration mechanisms
  [@cohen1990; @zahra2002].
- Learning favours **exploitation** over **exploration**, creating success and
  competency traps [@march1991; @levinthal1993]. Disruptive innovation is a vivid
  case [@christensen1997].
- **Ambidexterity**, structural, contextual, or sequential, is the main
  organizational answer, and is best seen as a leadership capability
  [@oreilly2013; @gibson2004].
:::

Table \@ref(tab:tab-dc-summary) presents the comparison of the chapter's theories.

```{r tab-dc-summary}
tibble::tribble(

  "Best-practice view (Eisenhardt & Martin)", "Process", "Effective processes create new resource configurations", "Simple rules outperform detailed routines in high-velocity markets", "Designing product-development and M&A processes",
  "Capability hierarchy and learning", "Routine", "Learning mechanisms modify operating routines", "Codification pays for infrequent, heterogeneous tasks", "Building integration playbooks",
  "Core rigidities", "Firm / project", "Strengths screen out misfit projects", "Incumbents struggle with competence-destroying change", "Diagnosing barriers to innovation",
  "Absorptive capacity", "Firm / unit", "Prior knowledge enables learning from outside", "Internal R&D raises returns to external knowledge", "Open innovation, alliance and M&A strategy",
  "Exploration and exploitation", "Organization", "Feedback favours sure, near returns", "Success and competency traps", "Portfolio and R&D allocation",
  "Ambidexterity", "Firm / business unit", "Separation plus integration, or supportive context", "Balanced, integrated firms outperform over time", "Organizing for innovation"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Comparison of the chapter's theories.")
```

## Discussion Questions {#dynamic-capabilities-questions}

1. Compare the Teece and the Eisenhardt-and-Martin views of dynamic capabilities.
   Which is more convincing for a software company in a high-velocity market, and
   which for a utility in a regulated market? Why?
2. Kodak had valuable resources and early knowledge of digital technology. Using
   the concepts of core rigidities, managerial cognition, and exploration versus
   exploitation, explain why this was not enough. What could have been done
   differently, and at what cost?
3. Design a study that measures dynamic capabilities *before* an environmental
   shock and tests whether they predict adaptation afterwards. What shock would you
   use, and how would you avoid defining the capability by its outcome?
4. A firm's open-innovation unit identifies many promising technologies but
   commercializes few. Using the potential/realized absorptive capacity
   distinction, diagnose the problem and propose remedies.
5. In the bandit simulation, the best exploration rate depends on how the
   environment changes. Translate this into a managerial rule of thumb for R&D
   portfolio allocation, and identify the indicators that should trigger a shift.
6. When would contextual ambidexterity be preferable to structural separation?
   Use an example from a function such as sales, operations, or HR.

## Further Reading {#dynamic-capabilities-reading}

- @teece1997: the founding statement of the dynamic capabilities framework,
  including processes, positions, and paths.
- @teece2007: the sensing-seizing-transforming framework and its microfoundations.
- @eisenhardt2000: the influential alternative view of dynamic capabilities as
  identifiable processes whose form depends on market dynamism.
- @winter2003 and @zollo2002: short, precise papers on what dynamic capabilities
  are and where they come from.
- @leonardbarton1992: the classic account of how core capabilities become core
  rigidities.
- @cohen1990 and @zahra2002: the foundational and the reconceptualized statements
  of absorptive capacity.
- @march1991: one of the most cited papers in organization science. Essential
  for understanding exploration and exploitation.
- @oreilly2013: an accessible review of ambidexterity research and its open
  questions.
